Key Takeaways

Nvidia's latest 13F shows $48.33 billion of US stocks, nearly all of it in SpaceX, Intel, CoreWeave, Coherent and Synopsys.

Analysts see 131% upside in CoreWeave, and 35% to 82% in the other four.

Jensen Huang's exit as Nvidia's CEO puts its backing of these companies in question.

If I could only buy one right now, it'd be Coherent, where earnings estimates are still rising.

Nvidia doesn't just sell the chips behind the AI buildout. It also owns big stakes in the companies doing the building, and its 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30, filed Nov. 16, shows $48.33 billion of US stocks across eight positions.

Those stakes matter more than usual right now. Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on Nov. 12, and The Wall Street Journal reported that interim CEO Colette Kress is expected to pull back on the computing deals and startup investments Nvidia has been financing.

Of Nvidia's positions worth 2% or more, these are the five where Wall Street sees the most upside: CoreWeave (CRWV:NASDAQ), SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ), Coherent (COHR:NYSE), Intel (INTC:NASDAQ) and Synopsys (SNPS:NASDAQ). Together, they made up nearly 98% of the portfolio at Sept. 30.

1. CoreWeave needs its lenders as much as its customers

Nvidia held 47.21 million CoreWeave shares worth $4.11 billion at Sept. 30, 8.5% of the portfolio and unchanged from June 30. Nvidia is also its chip supplier, a buyer of its capacity, and an investor that put in $2 billion at $87.20 a share in January. The stock has fallen 43% since Sept. 30, even after a third quarter that beat its own guidance, with revenue up 168% to $3.66 billion.

The worry is the bill for that growth: CoreWeave expects its next contract-backed loan to yield 7% to 7.5%. The consensus target has slipped from $130.54 a year ago, and a peak of $144.46 in August, to $115.34:

CoreWeave (CRWV): analysts' consensus (mean) price target, $ per share, last year (TIKR)

That's still 131% above the last close of $49.89, if CoreWeave can keep borrowing at a cost its contracts cover.

2. SpaceX is Nvidia's biggest bet, and it got bigger

SpaceX tops Nvidia's portfolio: 130.47 million shares worth $19.68 billion at Sept. 30, 40.7% of the total, after Nvidia added 6% more shares in the quarter. Of these five, it's the only stake Nvidia grew. The stock is down 6% since Sept. 30 and 37% below its 52-week high.

The expansion of the Guangzhou footprint to a contiguous 1,000 square kilometer area demonstrates the company's ability to move beyond isolated testing zones into large-scale, interconnected urban service areas.

Superior safety performance is being directly translated into financial gains, with insurance premiums for Gen 7 vehicles falling to 40% of the cost for human-driven taxis, down from 50% in the prior year.

The 'Joint Deployment Model' is being utilized as a capital-efficient international expansion strategy, leveraging partners like Uber and Verne to handle local operations and user acquisition while Pony AI provides the technology stack.

Robotruck revenue grew 76% year-over-year, primarily driven by freight transportation services through the Sinotrans collaboration, while the company also initiated Gen 4 commercial operations and expanded its project pipeline into major ports.

2027 Expansion and Efficiency Targets

Management is on track to meet its 2026 year-end targets of 3.5x Robotaxi revenue growth, a fleet size of 3,500 vehicles, and operations in 20 cities globally.

The 2027 strategic roadmap focuses on deepening operations in existing Tier 1 Chinese cities while accelerating penetration into high-value markets in Europe and the Middle East.

Robotruck operations are targeted to reach hundreds of vehicles across global ports by next year, transitioning from pilot programs to sustained transportation service revenue.

The company expects marginal R&D costs to decrease as the 'PonyWorld' simulation environment matures, allowing for rapid area extension without the need for extensive retraining or data collection.

Guidance assumes a continued shift toward a standardized national regulatory framework in China, which management believes will favor first-movers with established safety records.

Operational Efficiency and Financial Adjustments

The company reported a non-cash loss of $77 million due to changes in the fair value of trading securities, which significantly impacted the GAAP net loss for the quarter.

Capital expenditures decreased by 22% year-over-year, reflecting a disciplined investment pace even as the company supports mass production of its Gen 7 fleet.

The transition to automotive-grade chips for Gen 7 vehicles has successfully lowered bill-of-materials costs and energy consumption compared to general-purpose GPU setups.

Management highlighted the 15th Five-Year Plan in China as a critical policy tailwind that supports the large-scale commercial deployment of autonomous vehicles.

title: Former federal prosecutor weighs in on Nvidia’s legal strategy after Huang exit

Former federal prosecutor weighs in on Nvidia’s legal strategy after Huang exit
Luke Juricic

NVDA

Investing.com -- Nvidia's (NASDAQ:NVDA) decision to part ways with co-founder Jensen Huang appears driven by a legal containment strategy rather than boardroom panic. While activist investor Bill Ackman criticized directors this week for rushing to judgment and refusing to reinstate Huang, federal white-collar enforcement rules help explain why the board moved so quickly to protect shareholders as probes widen.

In an email Q&A with Investing.com, former federal prosecutor Evan J. Gotlob noted that "an immediate departure is often consistent with a company distancing itself from an individual and positioning itself to cooperate with investigators, although it is difficult to know the board's intent from the outside." Gotlob, who chairs the white-collar defense practice at DarrowEverett LLP, added that swift cooperation "signals a commitment to correcting the wrongdoing and can help shift responsibility toward the individuals involved rather than the organization as a whole."

That calculus follows overlapping scrutiny over Nvidia's Asian sales channels and Huang's undisclosed personal and workplace relationships. U.S. investigators and lawmakers have focused on billions of dollars in chip purchases tied to Singapore-based AI cloud firm Megaspeed International and former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspect of being a Chinese intelligence asset, an allegation Beijing and Megaspeed have denied. After media reports in early November exposed Jensen Huang's romantic relationship with Alice Huang, which he acknowledged in an employee memo shortly after, followed by separate reporting of an affair with an Nvidia vice president who reported directly to him, the board accepted his immediate resignation and has since ruled out his return. Directors also installed CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO, named Harvey C. Jones as Nvidia's first-ever independent chair, and formed a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee alongside an independent review led by outside counsel Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz.

Still, Gotlob cautioned that "cooperation does not guarantee leniency" and federal agencies will continue to "seek to recover the maximum damages available."
